lessons.title: ever, never, just, already, yet
lessons.art_alt: On a lilac path in the Whispering Forest, Lily holds open her explorer sticker book full of ticks and crosses, with a wooden signpost behind her and Sumi the little fox peeking out of her backpack

hook.text: Lily is exploring the Whispering Forest with Sumi the fox in her backpack. Her explorer book has a tick for every forest wonder she has seen, and a cross for the ones she hasn't seen. Today she wants to find a glowing mushroom! Five little words help us talk about things up to now: ever, never, just, already and yet. Let's try them.
hook.say: Lily is exploring the Whispering Forest with Sumi the fox in her backpack. Her explorer book has a tick for every forest wonder she has seen, and a cross for the ones she hasn't seen. Today she wants to find a glowing mushroom! Five little words help us talk about things up to now: ever, never, just, already and yet. Let's try them.

discover.text: Finish what the friends say. Drag the right little word into each gap, or tap it.
discover.hint: Questions about your whole life use ever. Not one time is never. A moment ago is just. Sooner than you thought is already. Still waiting is yet, at the end.

items.s: Sumi: “Have you ___ seen a glowing mushroom?”
items.why: Ever means at any time in your life. It fits questions: Have you ever seen …?

items.s: Lily: “No, I have ___ seen one. Not one time!”
items.why: Never means not one time, ever.

items.s: Pop! A mushroom has ___ lit up. Look, right now!
items.why: Just means a tiny moment ago.

items.s: Hoot has ___ found three. He was so quick!
items.why: Already means sooner than we expected.

items.s: Lily: “Has Gumdrop found one ___?”
items.why: Yet goes at the end of a question when we are still waiting to hear.

discover.say: Finish what the friends say. Drag the right little word into each gap, or tap it.

rule.text: Have or has plus a done-word, like seen or found, talks about time up to now. Ever means at any time, and we use it in questions. Never means not one time. Just means a moment ago. Already means sooner than we thought. Yet means up to now, and it goes at the end of questions and not-sentences.
examples: Have you ever seen a glowing mushroom?
I have never been to the forest at night.
A mushroom has just lit up.
Hoot has already found three.
Gumdrop hasn't found one yet.
rule.say: Have or has plus a done-word, like seen or found, talks about time up to now. Ever means at any time, and we use it in questions. Never means not one time. Just means a moment ago. Already means sooner than we thought. Yet means up to now, and it goes at the end of questions and not-sentences.
sayEx: Have you ever seen a glowing mushroom?
I have never been to the forest at night.
A mushroom has just lit up.
Hoot has already found three.
Gumdrop hasn't found one yet.

notes.Did ever: With ever about your life, we use have, not did: Have you ever eaten durian?
notes.Has: Has goes with he, she or it. With you, say have.

check.explain: Ask about someone's life with Have you ever …? So the gap needs Have.

check.q: Lily is still looking. She hasn't found a mushroom ___.

notes.already: Already is for something that has happened. She hasn't found one, so we're still waiting: yet.
notes.ever: Ever is for questions about your life, not for still waiting.

check.explain: She is still waiting to find one, so yet goes at the end: hasn't found one yet.
check.say: Lily is still looking. She hasn't found a mushroom blank.

options: I have just finished my snack.
I have finished just my snack.
I just have finished my snack.

That changes the meaning to only my snack. For a moment ago, just sits between have and the done-word.
Just goes after have: I have just finished.

check.explain: Just sits between have and the done-word: I have just finished, a moment ago.

reteach.text: Here's another way. Imagine a clock that points at right now. Just is one tick ago. Already is earlier than you expected. Yet is still waiting for it, so it comes at the end. Ever looks back over your whole life in a question. Never says zero times in your whole life. And the little words sit after have or has, except yet, which waits at the end.
examples: ⏱️ one tick ago → I have just eaten.
🏃 earlier than expected → She has already left.
⏳ still waiting → Has he come yet?
🌍 your whole life → Have you ever flown? I have never flown.

discover.text: Is each sentence right, or does it need fixing? Drag each card into a basket, or tap it and then a basket.
discover.hint: Ever is for questions. Yet goes at the end. Just and already sit after have or has.

items.t: Have you ever been to the zoo?
items.why: A question about your life: Have you ever …? Right!
Ever is for questions. Say: I have never seen snow, or Have you ever seen snow?
Just sits after has: she went out a moment ago. Right!
Yet goes at the end of a not-sentence: I haven't finished yet.
Already sits after have: we ate sooner than expected. Right!
Yet at the end of a not-sentence: we are still waiting. Right!

discover.say: Is each sentence right, or does it need fixing? Drag each card into a basket, or tap it and then a basket.

reteach.say: Here's another way. Imagine a clock that points at right now. Just is one tick ago. Already is earlier than you expected. Yet is still waiting for it, so it comes at the end. Ever looks back over your whole life in a question. Never says zero times in your whole life. And the little words sit after have or has, except yet, which waits at the end.

check2.q: Mum: “Do your homework!” Toby: “I have ___ done it! I finished before dinner.”

notes.yet: Yet is for questions and not-sentences, at the end. Toby has done it, sooner than Mum thought: already.
notes.ever: Ever is for questions about your life, not for homework that is finished.

check2.explain: He finished earlier than Mum expected, so he has already done it.
check2.say: Mum: “Do your homework!” Toby: “I have blank done it! I finished before dinner.”

options: Have you finished your book yet?
Have you yet finished your book?
Did you finished your book yet?

notes.Have you yet finished your book?: Yet waits at the end of the question: Have you finished your book yet?
notes.Did you finished your book yet?: After did, the verb stays plain, and for up to now we use have: Have you finished … yet?

check2.explain: Have + finished asks about up to now, and yet goes at the end.

check2.q: Gumdrop is scared of boats. She has ___ been on a boat.

notes.ever: Ever is for questions. In a sentence that means not one time, say never.
notes.just: Just means a moment ago. She's scared of boats, so she has not been on one.

check2.explain: Not one time in her life: she has never been on a boat.
check2.say: Gumdrop is scared of boats. She has blank been on a boat.

lessons.grown: 👪 Present perfect with ever / never / just / already / yet (B1 Preliminary): have/has + past participle for experience and for recent or expected events up to now. Word order: ever/never/just/already go between have and the participle; yet goes at the end of questions and negatives. Durian is a Singapore touch.

lessons.title: have done or did?

match.re: present perfect for a period|past simple with a finished time

lessons.art_alt: In a sunny glade of the Whispering Forest, Toby in a green cloak sits on a mossy log between a closed old diary with a pressed flower on it and an open treasure box full of sparkles, while Hoot the owl watches

hook.text: Toby and Hoot keep two kinds of memories. The old diary is closed: it holds days that are over, like yesterday. The sparkly treasure box is still open: it keeps filling up with things from up to now, like this week. Which memories go where? The time words tell us: did it, or have done it? Let's sort them.
hook.say: Toby and Hoot keep two kinds of memories. The old diary is closed: it holds days that are over, like yesterday. The sparkly treasure box is still open: it keeps filling up with things from up to now, like this week. Which memories go where? The time words tell us: did it, or have done it? Let's sort them.

discover.text: Sort the time words. Is the time finished and over, or does it reach up to now? Drag each card into a basket, or tap it and then a basket.
discover.hint: Ask: is this time over? Yesterday and last week are over. This week and so far are still going on.

items.why: Yesterday is over: I saw a deer yesterday.
Ever means any time in your life, up to now: Have you ever seen a deer?
Last week is over: We went camping last week.
So far means up to now: I have read two books so far.
2020 is finished: She learned to swim in 2020.
Yet means up to now: Have you finished yet?
Two days ago is a finished time: It rained two days ago.
This week isn't over: I have baked three cakes this week.

discover.say: Sort the time words. Is the time finished and over, or does it reach up to now? Drag each card into a basket, or tap it and then a basket.

rule.text: If you say WHEN it happened, and that time is finished, use the past: I went, she saw. Words like yesterday, last week, in 2020 and two days ago are finished times. If the time reaches up to now, use have or has plus the done-word: I have been, she has seen. Words like ever, yet, so far and this week reach up to now.
examples: I went to Sentosa last Sunday.
I have been to Sentosa three times so far.
Hoot baked a pie yesterday.
Hoot has baked two pies this week.
rule.say: If you say WHEN it happened, and that time is finished, use the past: I went, she saw. Words like yesterday, last week, in 2020 and two days ago are finished times. If the time reaches up to now, use have or has plus the done-word: I have been, she has seen. Words like ever, yet, so far and this week reach up to now.
sayEx: I went to Sentosa last Sunday.
I have been to Sentosa three times so far.
Hoot baked a pie yesterday.
Hoot has baked two pies this week.

check.q: We ___ the Botanic Gardens last Saturday.

notes.have visited: Last Saturday is a finished time, so we don't use have. Say visited.
notes.have visit: After have we need the done-word, and anyway last Saturday is over: visited.

check.explain: Last Saturday is over, so use the past: we visited.
check.say: We blank the Botanic Gardens last Saturday.

check.q: Sumi ___ three books so far this month.

notes.read: Read on its own is for a finished time, like last month. So far this month isn't over: has read.
notes.reads: Reads is for every day. So far needs has read.

check.explain: So far this month reaches up to now, so: Sumi has read three books.
check.say: Sumi blank three books so far this month.

options: I lost my hat two days ago.
I have lost my hat two days ago.
I have losed my hat two days ago.

Two days ago is a finished time. With a finished time we say lost, not have lost.
Losed isn't a word, and two days ago needs the past: lost.

check.explain: Two days ago is a finished time, so use the past: I lost my hat.

reteach.text: Here's another way. Think of two kinds of boxes, like Toby's diary and his treasure box. A closed box is a time that is over: yesterday, last week, in 2020. Put the past inside it: I went, I saw. An open box is a time that is still open, up to now: this week, so far, ever, yet. Put have or has inside it: I have been, I have seen. If you can say the exact finished time, the box is closed!
examples: 📦 closed box: I saw a rainbow yesterday.
📬 open box: I have seen two rainbows this week.
📦 closed box: She went to Malaysia in 2023.
📬 open box: Have you ever been to Malaysia?

discover.text: Closed box or open box? Drag the right words into each gap, or tap them.
discover.hint: Last Sunday and yesterday are closed boxes: went, baked. So far and this week are open: have been, has baked.

items.s: I ___ to Sentosa last Sunday.
items.why: Last Sunday is a closed box: I went.

items.s: I ___ to Sentosa three times so far.
items.why: So far is an open box, up to now: I have been.

items.s: Hoot ___ a cake yesterday.
items.why: Yesterday is a closed box: Hoot baked.

items.s: Hoot ___ two cakes this week.
items.why: This week is still open: Hoot has baked.

discover.say: Closed box or open box? Drag the right words into each gap, or tap them.

reteach.say: Here's another way. Think of two kinds of boxes, like Toby's diary and his treasure box. A closed box is a time that is over: yesterday, last week, in 2020. Put the past inside it: I went, I saw. An open box is a time that is still open, up to now: this week, so far, ever, yet. Put have or has inside it: I have been, I have seen. If you can say the exact finished time, the box is closed!

check2.q: ___ you ever been to the night safari?

notes.Did: With ever, the time is your whole life up to now, so use Have, not Did.
notes.Were: Were you … doesn't fit with been. Ask: Have you ever been …?

check2.explain: Ever reaches up to now, so we ask: Have you ever been …?
check2.say: blank you ever been to the night safari?

notes.has opened: In 2019 is a finished time, so we don't use has. Say opened.
notes.have opened: Crumb is one dragon, and 2019 is over: Crumb opened.

check2.explain: 2019 is finished, so use the past: Crumb opened the bakery in 2019.

check2.q: Which time words go with “I have seen …”?

notes.last night: Last night is over, so say I saw … last night.
notes.in 2021: 2021 is finished, so say I saw … in 2021.

check2.explain: So far this week reaches up to now: I have seen two owls so far this week.
check2.say: Which time words go with “I have seen …”?

lessons.grown: 👪 Present perfect vs past simple (B1 Preliminary). Past simple with finished-time expressions (yesterday, last week, in 2020, ago); present perfect with unfinished time and up-to-now words (ever, yet, so far, this week, today). The rule of thumb for children: if you can name the finished time, use the past. Singapore places (Sentosa, the Botanic Gardens, the Night Safari) give local context.

lessons.title: was doing when …
lessons.art_alt: Lily sits reading a green book on a pink picnic blanket under a big tree with a tiny fairy door, and looks up in surprise as Puffbun the white bunny pops out of the flower bushes

hook.text: Lily had a quiet picnic under the fairy-door tree in the Whispering Forest. She opened her storybook and read and read. Then, pop! Something jumped out of the bushes! When we tell a story, we need two kinds of past: the long thing that was going on, and the short thing that suddenly happened. Let's put Lily's afternoon on a timeline.
hook.say: Lily had a quiet picnic under the fairy-door tree in the Whispering Forest. She opened her storybook and read and read. Then, pop! Something jumped out of the bushes! When we tell a story, we need two kinds of past: the long thing that was going on, and the short thing that suddenly happened. Let's put Lily's afternoon on a timeline.

discover.text: Put each part of Lily's afternoon on the timeline: the start is at the top, the end is at the bottom. Drag a card, or tap it and then a place.
discover.hint: Lily has to sit down before she can read. Puffbun jumps out while she is reading, and the snack comes at the very end.

items.t: Lily sat down on her picnic blanket.
items.why: This is the start: first she sat down.
Was reading is the long part: the reading was still going on.

items.t: … when Puffbun jumped out of the bushes!
items.why: Jumped is the short, sudden thing. It happened in the middle of the reading.

items.t: Lily laughed and gave Puffbun a carrot.
items.why: This is the end: after the surprise, Lily shared her snack.

discover.say: Put each part of Lily's afternoon on the timeline: the start is at the top, the end is at the bottom. Drag a card, or tap it and then a place.

rule.text: Was or were plus an -ing word tells us about a long thing that was already going on: she was reading. The past, like jumped or rang, tells us about a short thing that happened in the middle of it. We join them with when: She was reading when Puffbun jumped out. With while, the long thing comes next: While she was reading, Puffbun jumped out.
examples: Lily was reading when Puffbun jumped out.
We were playing when it started to rain.
While Hoot was reading, the lamp went out.
rule.say: Was or were plus an -ing word tells us about a long thing that was already going on: she was reading. The past, like jumped or rang, tells us about a short thing that happened in the middle of it. We join them with when: She was reading when Puffbun jumped out. With while, the long thing comes next: While she was reading, Puffbun jumped out.
sayEx: Lily was reading when Puffbun jumped out.
We were playing when it started to rain.
While Hoot was reading, the lamp went out.

check.q: I ___ a bath when the phone rang.

notes.had: Had sounds like the bath was a quick short thing. The bath was going on, so: was having.
notes.am having: Am having is for now. This story is in the past: was having.

check.explain: The bath was the long thing going on, so: I was having a bath when the phone rang.
check.say: I blank a bath when the phone rang.

check.q: We were playing football when it ___ to rain.

notes.was starting: The rain starting is the short, sudden thing, so use the past: started.
notes.starts: Starts is for now or every day. The story is in the past: started.

check.explain: The football was going on, and the rain started suddenly: it started to rain.
check.say: We were playing football when it blank to rain.

options: While Puffbun was sleeping, the doorbell rang.
While Puffbun slept, the doorbell was ringing.
While Puffbun was sleep, the doorbell rang.

notes.While Puffbun slept, the doorbell was ri: This swaps them round: the sleeping was the long thing, and the ring was short. Say: was sleeping … rang.
notes.While Puffbun was sleep, the doorbell ra: After was we need the -ing word: was sleeping.

check.explain: The long thing gets was + -ing (was sleeping), and the short thing gets the past (rang).

reteach.text: Here's another way. Think of a movie. The long thing is the movie that is playing: Lily was reading, the rain was falling. Then a pop-up suddenly appears on the screen: Puffbun jumped out! The movie that keeps playing gets was or were plus -ing. The quick pop-up gets the past, like jumped, rang or fell.
examples: 🎬 the movie: Hoot was reading …
💥 the pop-up: … when the lamp went out.
🎬 the movie: They were singing …
💥 the pop-up: … when the bell rang.

discover.text: Movie or pop-up? Drag the right words into each gap, or tap them.
discover.hint: The long movie gets was or were + -ing. The quick pop-up gets the past.

items.s: I ___ when the lights went out.
items.why: Reading was the movie going on: was reading.

items.s: We were walking home when it ___ to rain.
items.why: The rain starting is the quick pop-up: started.

items.s: They ___ in the garden when Mum called them.
items.why: Playing was going on, and they is more than one: were playing.

items.s: Puffbun was sleeping when the doorbell ___.
items.why: The doorbell is the quick pop-up: rang.

discover.say: Movie or pop-up? Drag the right words into each gap, or tap them.

reteach.say: Here's another way. Think of a movie. The long thing is the movie that is playing: Lily was reading, the rain was falling. Then a pop-up suddenly appears on the screen: Puffbun jumped out! The movie that keeps playing gets was or were plus -ing. The quick pop-up gets the past, like jumped, rang or fell.

check2.q: Hoot ___ a story when the lamp went out.

notes.reads: Reads is for now or every day. The story is in the past: was reading.
notes.were reading: Hoot is one owl, so it's was, not were: was reading.

check2.explain: The reading was going on, so: Hoot was reading when the lamp went out.
check2.say: Hoot blank a story when the lamp went out.

check2.q: Sumi and Gumdrop were painting when the cat ___ the paint.

notes.was knocking over: Knocking the paint over is quick and sudden, so use the past: knocked over.
notes.knocks over: Knocks is for now. This happened in the past: knocked over.

check2.explain: The painting was going on, and the cat suddenly knocked over the paint.
check2.say: Sumi and Gumdrop were painting when the cat blank the paint.

check2.q: Which part was already going on? “When the bus came, Toby was eating a curry puff.”

notes.the bus coming: Came is the short, sudden thing. Was eating shows the long thing.
notes.nothing, both were quick: Was eating has was + -ing, so the eating was going on.

check2.explain: Was eating shows the eating was going on when the bus came.
check2.say: Which part was already going on? “When the bus came, Toby was eating a curry puff.”

lessons.grown: 👪 Past continuous vs past simple (B1 Preliminary): was/were + -ing for the longer background action, past simple for the shorter event that interrupts it, joined with when or while. The discovery reuses the 'order on a line' ladder from en.a2.freq as a timeline (sat down → reading → jumped out → snack); the re-teach is the 'movie and pop-up' picture. Curry puff is a Singapore touch.

lessons.title: if it rains, I will …
lessons.art_alt: On a lilac path in the Whispering Forest, Lily in a green raincoat and purple rain boots looks up at grey rain clouds with a finger on her chin, holding a closed yellow umbrella, next to a wooden signpost, with Sumi the cream fox smiling from her backpack

hook.text: Lily is walking down the forest path with Sumi the fox in her backpack. Uh oh, grey clouds are coming! Lily holds her yellow umbrella and thinks. Maybe it will rain, maybe it won't. When something might really happen, we talk about it with if. Let's help Lily plan.
hook.say: Lily is walking down the forest path with Sumi the fox in her backpack. Uh oh, grey clouds are coming! Lily holds her yellow umbrella and thinks. Maybe it will rain, maybe it won't. When something might really happen, we talk about it with if. Let's help Lily plan.

discover.text: Finish Lily's plans. Drag the right words into each gap, or tap them.
discover.hint: The maybe-part after if uses words like rains and is. The what-happens-next part uses will.

items.s: If it ___, Lily will open her yellow umbrella.
items.why: After if, use the present: if it rains. We don't say if it will rain.

items.s: If it rains, Lily ___ her umbrella.
items.why: This part says what happens next, so it gets will: will open.

items.s: If Sumi jumps in a puddle, she ___ wet!
items.why: Getting wet is what happens next: she will get wet.

items.s: If the path ___ muddy, Lily's rain boots will keep her feet dry.
items.why: The maybe-part after if uses the present: if the path is muddy.

items.s: If Lily ___ the signpost, she will find the way home.
items.why: After if, use the present. Lily is one girl, so: if Lily follows.

discover.say: Finish Lily's plans. Drag the right words into each gap, or tap them.

rule.text: When something might really happen, use if plus the present for the maybe-part: if it rains. Then use will plus a verb for what happens next: I will open my umbrella. Will never goes right after if. The two parts can swap places: I will open my umbrella if it rains. When the if-part comes first, put a comma after it.
examples: If it rains, I will open my umbrella.
If Sumi is hungry, she will eat a berry.
We will get wet if we don't hurry.
rule.say: When something might really happen, use if plus the present for the maybe-part: if it rains. Then use will plus a verb for what happens next: I will open my umbrella. Will never goes right after if. The two parts can swap places: I will open my umbrella if it rains. When the if-part comes first, put a comma after it.
sayEx: If it rains, I will open my umbrella.
If Sumi is hungry, she will eat a berry.
We will get wet if we don't hurry.

check.q: If it ___ tomorrow, we will stay at home.

notes.will rain: After if, we don't use will. Say: If it rains tomorrow.
notes.rained: Rained is for the past. Tomorrow's rain might really happen, so use the present: rains.

check.explain: The maybe-part after if takes the present, even for tomorrow: If it rains tomorrow.
check.say: If it blank tomorrow, we will stay at home.

check.q: If you water the plant every day, it ___.

notes.grow: This part says what happens next, so it needs will: it will grow.
notes.growing: Growing can't stand alone here. Say what will happen: it will grow.

check.explain: Watering is the maybe-part, and growing is what happens next, so: it will grow.
check.say: If you water the plant every day, it blank.

options: If Sumi is hungry, she will eat a berry.
If Sumi will be hungry, she will eat a berry.
If Sumi is hungry, she eat a berry.

notes.If Sumi will be hungry, she will eat a b: Will doesn't go right after if. Say: If Sumi is hungry.
The next-part needs will: she will eat a berry.

check.explain: Present after if (is hungry), and will for what happens next (will eat).

reteach.text: Here's another way. Think of a weather card cut into two halves. The first half is the maybe: if it rains, if you are late. It uses the present, like rains or are. The second half is what happens then: will plus a verb, like will open or will miss. Will only lives on the second half, never next to if.
examples: 🌧️ maybe: If it rains, ☂️ then: I will open my umbrella.
⏰ maybe: If you are late, 🚌 then: you will miss the bus.
☀️ maybe: If it is sunny, 🏖️ then: we will go to East Coast Park.

discover.text: Is each sentence right, or does it need fixing? Drag each card into a basket, or tap it and then a basket.
discover.hint: Check the if-half: no will there. Then check the other half: it needs will.

items.t: If it's sunny, we will go to East Coast Park.
items.why: Present after if, will for what happens next. Right!

items.t: If it will rain, I will stay inside.
items.why: No will after if. Say: If it rains, I will stay inside.

items.t: If you are late, you will miss the bus.
items.why: Are late is the maybe, will miss is what happens. Right!

items.t: If he practises, he win the race.
items.why: The next-part needs will: If he practises, he will win the race.

items.t: We will have ice cream if we finish early.
items.why: The halves swapped places, and it's still right!

items.t: If she will call, I will answer.
items.why: No will after if. Say: If she calls, I will answer.

discover.say: Is each sentence right, or does it need fixing? Drag each card into a basket, or tap it and then a basket.

reteach.say: Here's another way. Think of a weather card cut into two halves. The first half is the maybe: if it rains, if you are late. It uses the present, like rains or are. The second half is what happens then: will plus a verb, like will open or will miss. Will only lives on the second half, never next to if.

check2.q: If we ___ now, we will catch the MRT.

notes.will leave: Will doesn't go right after if. Say: If we leave now.
notes.left: Left is the past. This is a real plan for now, so use the present: leave.

check2.explain: The if-part uses the present: If we leave now, we will catch the train.
check2.say: If we blank now, we will catch the MRT.

check2.q: If you eat too much cake, you ___ a tummy ache.

notes.will got: After will, use the plain verb: will get, not will got.
notes.are get: Are get isn't English. What happens next needs will: will get.

check2.explain: The tummy ache is what happens next, so it gets will plus the plain verb: will get.
check2.say: If you eat too much cake, you blank a tummy ache.

check2.q: Lily saves \$2 every week. If she saves for five weeks, she ___ \$10.

notes.will has: After will, the verb stays plain, even with she: will have.
notes.has will: The order is will first, then the verb: will have.

check2.explain: Saving is the maybe-part, and having ten dollars is what happens next: she will have \$10.
check2.say: Lily saves 2 dollars every week. If she saves for five weeks, she blank 10 dollars.

lessons.grown: 👪 First conditional (B1 Preliminary): if + present simple, will + bare infinitive, for real and possible future situations. No will in the if-clause; the clauses can swap, with a comma when the if-clause comes first. Singapore touches: East Coast Park, the MRT and saving in Singapore dollars.

lessons.title: if I were a bird …

match.re: second conditional|imaginary present|if I were you

lessons.art_alt: Lily sits at a mossy log in the Whispering Forest with her chin in her hands, smiling and daydreaming, next to Sumi the cream fox, while a dream bubble shows her with bird wings flying over pink and green treetops with little brown birds

hook.text: Lily rests her chin on a mossy log and starts to daydream. In her dream bubble she has bird wings, and she flies over the treetops with the little birds! But Lily doesn't really have wings. Some if-sentences are about things that could really happen. Others are only imagined, like a dream. Let's sort them.
hook.say: Lily rests her chin on a mossy log and starts to daydream. In her dream bubble she has bird wings, and she flies over the treetops with the little birds! But Lily doesn't really have wings. Some if-sentences are about things that could really happen. Others are only imagined, like a dream. Let's sort them.

discover.text: Could it really happen, or is it only a dream? Drag each card into a basket, or tap it and then a basket.
discover.hint: Look at the second half. Will means it could really happen. Would means it's only imagined.

items.t: If it rains, I will open my umbrella.
items.why: Rain can really happen: if + present, will.

items.t: If I had wings, I would fly.
items.why: Lily has no wings. It's a dream: if + had, would.

items.t: If Sumi is hungry, she will eat a berry.
items.why: Sumi can really get hungry: is, will.

items.t: If I were a bird, I would sing all day.
items.why: Lily isn't a bird. It's imagined: were, would.

items.t: If we hurry, we will catch the bus.
items.why: Hurrying can really happen: hurry, will.

items.t: If I lived in a castle, I would keep a dragon.
items.why: Lily doesn't live in a castle. It's a dream: lived, would.

discover.say: Could it really happen, or is it only a dream? Drag each card into a basket, or tap it and then a basket.

rule.text: For things that are not true now, like a dream, use if plus a past word, like had or lived, and would plus a verb: If I had wings, I would fly. It isn't about yesterday. It's an imagined now. With I, he, she and it, we say were: If I were a bird. And If I were you, I would … is a kind way to give advice.
examples: If I had wings, I would fly over the trees.
If I were a bird, I would sing all day.
If I were you, I would take an umbrella.
rule.say: For things that are not true now, like a dream, use if plus a past word, like had or lived, and would plus a verb: If I had wings, I would fly. It isn't about yesterday. It's an imagined now. With I, he, she and it, we say were: If I were a bird. And If I were you, I would … is a kind way to give advice.
sayEx: If I had wings, I would fly over the trees.
If I were a bird, I would sing all day.
If I were you, I would take an umbrella.

check.q: Lily isn't a bird. If she ___ a bird, she would fly to school.

notes.is: Is is for real things now. She isn't a bird, so it's imagined: if she were.
notes.will be: Will doesn't go after if, and this is a dream: if she were.

check.explain: It's only imagined, so the if-part steps back to were: If she were a bird.
check.say: Lily isn't a bird. If she blank a bird, she would fly to school.

check.q: If I had a magic carpet, I ___ to the moon.

notes.will fly: Will is for things that could really happen. A magic carpet is a dream: would fly.
notes.fly: The dream-part needs would: I would fly.

check.explain: Had a magic carpet is a dream, so the other half uses would: I would fly.
check.say: If I had a magic carpet, I blank to the moon.

options: If I lived under the sea, I would swim with the fish.
If it is sunny, we will swim.
If you are cold, I will close the window.

A sunny day can really happen. See the will?
notes.If you are cold, I will close the window: Being cold can really happen, so it uses will.

check.explain: Nobody really lives under the sea, so it's a dream: lived, would.

reteach.text: Here's another way. Think of two bubbles. A real bubble holds things that could really happen, and it uses will. A dream bubble floats above your head and holds things that are not true. Inside a dream bubble, every word takes one step back: have becomes had, am becomes were, and will becomes would.
examples: 💭 I don't have wings. → If I had wings, I would fly.
💭 I'm not a bird. → If I were a bird, I would sing.
💡 kind advice: If I were you, I would wear a jacket.

discover.text: Fill the dream bubbles. Drag the right words into each gap, or tap them.
discover.hint: In a dream, have steps back to had, am steps back to were, and will steps back to would.

items.s: If I ___ wings, I would fly over the trees.
items.why: I don't have wings, so have steps back to had.

items.s: If Sumi were as big as a horse, she ___ carry Lily.
items.why: It's a dream, so will steps back to would.

items.s: If I ___ you, I would wear a jacket.
items.why: I can't be you! For I, he, she and it in a dream, we say were.

items.s: If we ___ on the moon, we would jump very high.
items.why: We don't live on the moon, so live steps back to lived.

discover.say: Fill the dream bubbles. Drag the right words into each gap, or tap them.

reteach.say: Here's another way. Think of two bubbles. A real bubble holds things that could really happen, and it uses will. A dream bubble floats above your head and holds things that are not true. Inside a dream bubble, every word takes one step back: have becomes had, am becomes were, and will becomes would.

check2.q: Your friend is sad. “If I ___ you, I would say sorry to her.”

notes.am: You can't really be your friend, so it's imagined: If I were you.
notes.would be: Would goes in the other half, not after if: If I were you.

check2.explain: If I were you, I would … is the kind way to give advice.
check2.say: Your friend is sad. “If I blank you, I would say sorry to her.”

check2.q: Toby doesn't have a bike. If he had a bike, he ___ to school.

notes.will ride: He has no bike, so it's a dream, not a plan: would ride.
notes.rides: Rides is for real every day. In a dream, say would ride.

check2.explain: Toby has no bike, so it's imagined: had a bike, would ride.
check2.say: Toby doesn't have a bike. If he had a bike, he blank to school.

check2.q: If Lily found \$100, she ___ give it to a police officer.

notes.will: After found, the dream-part needs would, not will.
notes.was: Was give isn't English. The dream-part needs would + verb.

check2.explain: Finding \$100 is imagined, so the other half uses would: she would give it back.
check2.say: If Lily found 100 dollars, she blank give it to a police officer.

lessons.grown: 👪 Second conditional (B1 Preliminary): if + past simple, would + bare infinitive, for imagined or unlikely present and future situations; were for all persons (If I were …), including advice (If I were you, I would …). The discovery sorts real (first conditional) vs imagined (second conditional) by will / would.

lessons.title: the cake was eaten
lessons.art_alt: On a pink checked picnic blanket in the Whispering Forest, Lily kneels with her hands on her cheeks in surprise beside an empty plate with only cake crumbs, while Puffbun the round pink bunny sits next to it with crumbs on its cheek and Sumi the fox giggles in Lily's backpack

hook.text: Lily and Sumi had a picnic with a big slice of cake. Lily looked away for one minute. When she looked back, the plate was empty! Only crumbs were left. Oh no, the cake was eaten! Hmm, look at Puffbun's cheek. Sumi giggles. Sometimes what happened to a thing matters more than who did it. Let's tell the story.
hook.say: Lily and Sumi had a picnic with a big slice of cake. Lily looked away for one minute. When she looked back, the plate was empty! Only crumbs were left. Oh no, the cake was eaten! Hmm, look at Puffbun's cheek. Sumi giggles. Sometimes what happened to a thing matters more than who did it. Let's tell the story.

discover.text: Tell the cake story. Drag the right words into each gap, or tap them.
discover.hint: One thing takes was or is. Many things take were or are. By tells us who did it.

items.s: Oh no! The cake ___!
items.why: The cake didn't eat anything. Something happened to it: it was eaten.

items.s: The cake ___ by Crumb this morning.
items.why: Crumb did the baking, and the cake is one thing: was baked.

items.s: Crumbs ___ on Puffbun's cheek!
items.why: Crumbs are many, so it's were: were found.

items.s: Cakes ___ at Crumb's bakery every day.
items.why: Every day is now, and cakes are many: are sold.

items.s: The cake was eaten ___ Puffbun!
items.why: By tells us who did it: by Puffbun.

discover.say: Tell the cake story. Drag the right words into each gap, or tap them.

rule.text: In the passive, the thing that something happens to comes first. Then comes was or were for the past, or is or are for now, plus a done-word like eaten, baked or found: The cake was eaten. To say who did it, add by: The cake was eaten by Puffbun. It means the same as Puffbun ate the cake, but now the spotlight is on the cake.
examples: Puffbun ate the cake. → The cake was eaten by Puffbun.
The cupcakes were baked this morning.
Bread is sold at the bakery.
rule.say: In the passive, the thing that something happens to comes first. Then comes was or were for the past, or is or are for now, plus a done-word like eaten, baked or found: The cake was eaten. To say who did it, add by: The cake was eaten by Puffbun. It means the same as Puffbun ate the cake, but now the spotlight is on the cake.
sayEx: Puffbun ate the cake., The cake was eaten by Puffbun.
The cupcakes were baked this morning.
Bread is sold at the bakery.

check.q: The window ___ by the wind last night.

notes.broke: The window didn't break something. It had something done to it: was broken.
notes.was break: After was, use the done-word: broken, not break.

check.explain: The wind did it to the window, so: the window was broken by the wind.
check.say: The window blank by the wind last night.

notes.is made: Biscuits are many, so use are, not is: are made.
notes.make: The biscuits don't make anything. Somebody makes them: they are made.

check.explain: Many biscuits, and it's true now: they are made in Singapore.

check.q: Which sentence means the same as “Hoot wrote the letter”?
options: The letter was written by Hoot.
Hoot was written by the letter.

A letter can't write! The letter comes first and then was written.
This swaps them round. Hoot did the writing: by Hoot.

check.explain: The letter comes first, then was written, then by Hoot, who did it.
check.say: Which sentence means the same as “Hoot wrote the letter”?

reteach.text: Here's another way. Think of a spotlight on a stage. In a normal sentence, the spotlight shines on the doer first: Puffbun ate the cake. In the passive, we turn the spotlight onto the thing first: The cake was eaten. The doer can stay in the dark, or come back at the end with by: by Puffbun.
examples: 🔦 doer first: Puffbun ate the cake.
🔦 thing first: The cake was eaten by Puffbun.
🔦 doer first: Lily washed the plates.
🔦 thing first: The plates were washed.

discover.text: Where is the spotlight? On the doer first, or on the thing first? Drag each card into a basket, or tap it and then a basket.
discover.hint: Was, were, is or are plus a done-word means the thing comes first.

items.why: Puffbun did it, and Puffbun comes first.
The cake comes first, with was eaten.
Lily did the washing, and she comes first.

items.t: The plates were washed by Lily.
items.why: The plates come first, and by Lily comes at the end.
Sumi did the finding, and Sumi comes first.
The stone comes first, with was found.

discover.say: Where is the spotlight? On the doer first, or on the thing first? Drag each card into a basket, or tap it and then a basket.

reteach.say: Here's another way. Think of a spotlight on a stage. In a normal sentence, the spotlight shines on the doer first: Puffbun ate the cake. In the passive, we turn the spotlight onto the thing first: The cake was eaten. The doer can stay in the dark, or come back at the end with by: by Puffbun.

check2.q: After the picnic, the plates ___ by Lily.

notes.was washed: Plates are many, so use were: were washed.
notes.washed: The plates didn't wash anything. They had it done to them: were washed.

check2.explain: The plates come first and they are many, so: the plates were washed by Lily.
check2.say: After the picnic, the plates blank by Lily.

notes.speaks: English can't speak! People speak it, so: English is spoken.
notes.is speak: After is, use the done-word: spoken.

check2.explain: People speak it, and English comes first: English is spoken.

check2.q: Put the spotlight on the fence: “Toby painted the fence.”
options: The fence was painted by Toby.
Toby was painted by the fence.

It needs was before the done-word: was painted.
This swaps them round. Toby did the painting: by Toby.

check2.explain: The fence comes first, then was painted, then by Toby at the end.
check2.say: Put the spotlight on the fence: “Toby painted the fence.”

lessons.grown: 👪 Passive voice (B1 Preliminary): present and past simple passive, is/are/was/were + past participle, with an optional by-agent; used when the thing affected matters more than the doer. The re-teach sorts active (doer first) and passive (thing first) word order.
